posts.author: ISC
posts.body:
It's all about sharing. People share their creations to get feedback, advice, and improve themselves. But it's not a one-way process; you can also be amazed by what others are able to create and share. Whether it's graphics, programming, or music, everyone contributes their art, allowing the entire community to grow and appreciate the RPG Maker world.
In the indie scene, games are often made by individuals, but the reality is that reaching the final project often involves seeking feedback from testers and players, or asking advice from those more experienced in certain areas or better at fixing bugs. Making games is a collaborative effort.
This is my opinion, though I could be wrong

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
Several reasons:
1.  I still tinker with my own game and RPG Maker is my "engine of choice" for doing so (I like the ease of use and the style of the RTP graphics), so there's always useful information here or even resources.  I tend to learn about one new thing a week here, even if I don't use it (or forget it later!).
2.  I enjoy trying to help people or give advice.  Especially about game design.  The only downside to that on these forums is that only the "newbies" tend to be here to "learn something".  Everyone else is trying to "teach something", so it's easy to clash over design philosophy and other game design elements.  It creates a place where few people are "open minded", but at the same time, becomes a pretty good resource for a lot of new users.  I'm not a fan of the "the forums are nothing but teachers", but I do like the, "if you have a problem, basically everyone here can help you, will help you, and probably give you at least half a dozen different perspectives on whatever your problem is".  Anyway, to get off that tangent, I've always liked teaching people things, so I stick around on the off-chance I can teach something.
3.  Nostalgia.  I used to have one or two friends on here who were really great at debate.  Conversations with them rarely devolved into insults and often stuck with hammering home facts and figures and hypotheticals.  Made me reconsider a lot of my early game design decisions or even stances on things.  I miss them and miss those interactions.  These two people were probably the only people on these forums to ever consistently prove me wrong and give my brain a real workout.  So, I'm basically just "holding the torch" for my old friends (maybe they didn't even consider me a friend, I don't know) in hopes they will come back or someone will come in to take their place.
4.  I've been here long enough to have seen gaming opinions shift in quite drastic directions.  It's kind of fun to watch.  Opinions I held years ago and were shouted down by the majority of the users are now "the mainstream way to think".  I used to say that mini-games in an RPG were a waste of time, and there are far more users who agree with that sentiment (or a variation of that sentiment) today than there were 10 years ago (or more) when I joined.  People have even come around on crafting systems and what little they add to an RPG other than grind.  It's sort of fun to watch people's opinions on things change over the course of years and feel "in the middle" of that change.  Or, sometimes, "ahead" of that change.  It's a fun feeling to go, "man, I was super ahead of the curve" when things do change like that.
5.  Finally...  Sometimes someone creates a genuinely interesting discussion or topic.  I'm partial to Game Mechanics Design for these things, but I'll take anything that sounds remotely interesting.  This is not to be confused with my "pity posts", where I arrive like super late to a topic and post something just 'cause I'm bored, and want to see if what I say kicks the conversation back into relevency for the users or not.  But, if I get in on the ground floor of a topic (usually a reply on the first page), then I find the potential for interesting and intellectual debate on it to be pretty high.  Though, if everyone is just "I agree", then... the topic dies.  Which... makes the topic not interesting at all anymore.

I don't remember if I've ever said this before or not:
If you only take feedback from your customers, the project quality could suffer.
As George Carlin says:
"It isn't enough to know which notes to play, you need to know WHY THEY NEED TO BE PLAYED".
It can generally be dangerous to only listen to feedback from one specific group and only that specific group.
After all, I'd trust the editing of any of my stories to an actual editor who knows what they're doing... rather than "random audience member who wants me to change the editing".  But, I'm not going to trust "professional editor" to tell me if "the story is enjoyable" or not... I'll leave that to the person buying the story.
Professionals can help you make your stuff look, feel, and BE professional (IE:  Raise the quality of what is there).  Your audience can only give you general feedback on what is and is not fun, but rarely ever why, or how to fix it.

Unless something crazy happens (which, knowing RPG Maker websites is totally possible), I'll probably be here to stay. Though, I will say that if I start heading towards RPG Architect or some other engine more I won't be coming back here much... just because it's off topic and I've got other places online I like to socialize. I don't know though, something about RPG Maker is just really cozy.

posts.author: ISC
posts.body:
AquaEcho said:
What is the end goal though?...
Click to expand...
Creating games mainly comes from a passion, and many do it as a hobby, simply for the joy of making something fun for themselves and others. Can this hobby turn into a job? Absolutely yes, but it requires time, learning, and above all, feedback from those who understand what it means to experience that emotion. In a place like this, you can grow and learn, primarily to improve what you create with your passion. The commercial aspect may come later, or it may remain a hobby forever.
Since I started, I’ve seen many talented people take their first small steps and go on to become well-known or, at the very least, achieve their own sense of fulfillment. All of these people started from passion, without commercial goals. Does selling your creation really have to be the sole and ultimate goal? Can’t we just create because it’s something we enjoy doing?
